segments.text: Three ways to delete data: DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP.
SQL gives you three tools to remove data, and each one works at a different level.
DELETE removes some rows: the ones its WHERE picks. TRUNCATE removes all the rows, but keeps the empty table.
DROP removes the table itself.
DELETE is DML. Here it removes one student: S zero three, Eva Sanz.
Enrolment's foreign key says ON DELETE CASCADE, so Eva's two enrolments are deleted with her.
DELETE works row by row, and fires the delete triggers of the table. Without a WHERE, it removes every row.
But nothing is final until COMMIT: Oracle keeps the undo, so ROLLBACK brings all three rows back.
TRUNCATE is DDL. It takes no WHERE: it empties the whole table at once.
Instead of deleting row by row, Oracle simply frees the table's storage, so it is very fast, and no triggers fire. The columns, constraints and indexes stay.
Like every DDL statement, it commits. ROLLBACK cannot bring the rows back.
And you cannot truncate a parent table. Enrolment is empty now, but its foreign key to student is still enabled, so Oracle refuses: O R A zero two two six six.
Disable the foreign key first, or use DELETE.
DROP TABLE removes everything: the rows, the columns, and the table's indexes and constraints.
In Oracle a dropped table goes to the recycle bin, like a file on your desktop.
FLASHBACK TABLE, TO BEFORE DROP, brings it back, rows included.
Add PURGE, and the table skips the bin: it is gone for good.
Dropping a parent table that others still reference fails, with O R A zero two four four nine.
CASCADE CONSTRAINTS also drops the foreign keys that point to it. The enrolment rows stay, but nothing checks them any more.
To sum up. DELETE is DML: it can filter with WHERE, fires triggers, and can be rolled back.
TRUNCATE and DROP are DDL: no WHERE, no triggers, and an implicit commit. TRUNCATE keeps the empty table; DROP removes it, unless you flash it back.
When in doubt, DELETE, and check before you COMMIT.
